The fixed queue and resumable state are in ignored `work/overnight-ingest-2026-10-10/queue.json`; originals remain in ignored `ingest/`. Files are processed one at a time in filename order. **Corrections and interpretation.** The writeup overstates that `post-merge` runs whenever `git pull` is issued. Its successful example is a fast-forward; upstream source separates the already-current return path, and the hook manual excludes conflicted merges. Rebase is a different integration mode. The screenshots include making the local hook executable, which matters on Linux. Modern repository-ownership checks and effective configuration must be assessed before transferring the historical sudo result to another host. A GitLab Developer label alone does not establish the effective rights on every project/branch. Deployment of an HTML comment confirms content propagation, while the later PHP callback is separate execution evidence. A database running in Docker does not by itself prove that the caller lacks client binaries or establish the caller's network namespace. The screenshot's password happens to resemble base64; the observed SSH command uses the original value, so no decoding rule was imported. Replacing `jne` with `je` reverses a condition rather than universally bypassing a username check; the screenshot shows local `su` success, not proof that root SSH login is enabled.

**Reviewed without additional skills.** Existing Nmap, Gobuster, SSH/SCP, listener and binary-inspection coverage handles the repeated tool uses. The JavaScript bookmark and GitLab browser actions are application context, not a reason to execute copied code or add a generic Linux tool skill. Ghidra and x32dbg are demonstrated through GUI/Windows actions; no Linux command-line equivalent was asserted. The PHP reverse shell, privilege-escalation hook and credential replay were reviewed as source context but neither executed nor packaged as default workflows.

| New `derby-ij` | 7â€“9 motivate inspection of an embedded application database with ij. The portable adaptation uses a consistent working copy, read-only SQL, schema-qualified metadata and bounded column selection, with display/lock/driver recovery decisions. |
| Enriched `hashcat` | 10â€“13 support verifying legacy OFBiz salt-before-password SHA-1 and converting unpadded base64url. The converter preserves UTF-8 salt bytes as hex and requires `--hex-salt` for mode 120, rejects malformed/noncanonical input and refuses to overwrite an existing output. |

The catalogue now contains **105 independently installable skills**. The new decision examples are labelled illustrative. The Hashcat helper remains an inline conversion in the skill; no runtime dependency on another skill or maintenance file was added. The earlier Hashcat source footer is retained below.

**Corrections and interpretation.** The many 404 child paths on page 3 do not themselves prove exposed content; the later parent/login response is separate evidence. The source's use of `-k` disables certificate validation and does not justify making it a default. Modern Feroxbuster link extraction and recursion are separate controls; `--depth 0` is unlimited, and rate limits apply per directory. The documentation's older threads/connection wording was reconciled against the current CLI/parser rather than generalized into an overall rate guarantee. Derby can run embedded or as a network server; the case's absence of a listening database port is not a product-wide restriction. Page 8's `tar cvf` makes an archive without compression, and an ordinary copy of a running database is not a guaranteed consistent backup. `READONLY ON` governs the SQL connection and does not promise zero filesystem writes while booting/recovering a working copy. Page 7's configured default hash algorithm alone does not identify all stored records. The legacy source hashes salt bytes before password bytes; base64url spelling, padding and digest length matter. The published digest converts to `b8fd3f41a541a435857a8f3e751cc3a91c174362`, with literal salt `d` represented as hex `64` by the new procedure. General SHA-1 collision weakness does not by itself explain password recovery; candidate coverage and verification cost still matter. A recovered database value and successful local `su` in the historical case do not establish other accounts' current authentication behavior.

**Reviewed without additional skills.** Nmap, curl, tar, base64, tcpdump, ysoserial and existing configuration/source inspection guidance already cover the repeated portable decisions. The OFBiz exploit delivery, reverse callback, global Java alternative changes, raw netcat transfer and root credential replay were read as case context; no such commands were executed or added as default tool workflows. A product-specific exploitation skill and a general Derby administration/backup procedure were deliberately left outside this bounded intake; all related pages were nevertheless read.

**Primary sources.** Feroxbuster's [CLI reference](https://epi052.github.io/feroxbuster-docs/configuration/command-line/), [option parser](https://github.com/epi052/feroxbuster/blob/main/src/parser.rs) and [thread-limit explanation](https://epi052.github.io/feroxbuster-docs/configuration/threads-and-limits/) were checked for expansion, rate, output, TLS and resume semantics. Derby's [connection command](https://db.apache.org/derby/docs/10.13/tools/rtoolsijcomref22318.html), [driver selection](https://db.apache.org/derby/docs/10.16/tools/ttoolsij97656.html), [metadata listing](https://db.apache.org/derby/docs/10.4/tools/rtoolsijcomrefshow.html), [Describe](https://db.apache.org/derby/docs/10.4/tools/rtoolsijcomrefdescribe.html), [Readonly](https://db.apache.org/derby/docs/10.4/tools/rtoolsijcomref61092.html), [MaximumDisplayWidth](https://db.apache.org/derby/docs/10.4/tools/rtoolsijcomref12281.html), [FETCH FIRST](https://db.apache.org/derby/docs/10.16/ref/rrefsqljoffsetfetch.html), [backup overview](https://db.apache.org/derby/docs/10.9/adminguide/cadminbckupdb.html) and [offline-copy requirements](https://db.apache.org/derby/docs/10.9/adminguide/cadminhubbkup12677.html) support the inspection procedure. The historical [OFBiz HashCrypt source](https://github.com/apache/ofbiz-framework/blob/release18.12/framework/base/src/main/java/org/apache/ofbiz/base/crypto/HashCrypt.java), [Hashcat mode 120 implementation](https://github.com/hashcat/hashcat/blob/master/src/modules/module_00120.c), [Hashcat CLI reference](https://hashcat.net/wiki/doku.php?id=hashcat) and [Python base64 API](https://docs.python.org/3/library/base64.html) support the conversion and explicit hex-salt handling. These are documentation/source reviews, not installed-version observations.

**Corrections and interpretation.** The synopsis skips the password-reset stage between the initial support identity and access to the forensic share; pages 6â€“7 supply that missing step. Profile-directory names are candidate usernames, and a whitespace-split SMB listing can include headers, dot entries or truncated names; existing LDAP/GetNPUsers guidance already distinguishes candidates from verified principals. The no-preauthentication requests shown on page 4 are not password guesses. Its grep filter discards error context, which should be preserved. Page 5 mentions a rockyou run, while the displayed John command has no explicit wordlist; no candidate-list coverage was inferred from the prose. The BloodHound screenshot identifies a ForceChangePassword relationship; this is a reset operation, not evidence of merely knowing the old password. Existing collector guidance already handles legacy/CE differences and limits of the alternate DNS option.

Page 8's parser output contains NT/SHA values, not a demonstrated plaintext password. Separately sorting names and NT values on page 9 loses their associations and creates unnecessary ambiguity. The observed default `lockoutThreshold: 0` does not establish every user's effective fine-grained policy or unlimited application retries. Modern OpenLDAP guidance uses an explicit URI, authenticated transport and valid presence filter rather than importing the historical `-h`/`-p`, command-line password and standalone `*` filter. A recovered value remains snapshot evidence until a separate authorised validation establishes its current use. The denied file copy and the note on page 10 suggest encryption in that case; access denial alone does not prove EFS. The backup versions shown in prose and screenshots differ, so a recovery procedure must select the actual acquired version rather than copy the date. Page 16 demonstrates that SAM account records, cached domain verifiers and LSA secrets are distinct results. A machine's present role alone also does not prove which historical database artifacts may exist in its acquired files.

**Reviewed without additional skills.** Existing Nmap, Samba smbclient, GetNPUsers, John, BloodHound.py, Evil-WinRM and offline-NTDS instructions cover the repeated useful tasks. The rpcclient reset, CrackMapExec credential trials, Samba service/account configuration, WBAdmin/DiskShadow/SeBackupPrivilege acquisition and remote WMI/PSExec execution were read as case context. No such actions were performed. A standalone rpcclient skill for controlled account changes and Windows backup/EFS administration would need a separately scoped procedure and validation; they were deliberately deferred instead of turning a destructive historical chain into a default Linux utility workflow. This is a material-scope decision, not partial page coverage.

**Primary sources.** Reviewed Pypykatz's [project scope](https://github.com/skelsec/pypykatz), [LSA CLI and output handling](https://github.com/skelsec/pypykatz/blob/main/pypykatz/lsadecryptor/cmdhelper.py), [MSV/session structure](https://github.com/skelsec/pypykatz/blob/main/pypykatz/lsadecryptor/packages/msv/decryptor.py) and [core parser/result serialization](https://github.com/skelsec/pypykatz/blob/main/pypykatz/pypykatz.py). Impacket's [secretsdump CLI](https://github.com/fortra/impacket/blob/master/examples/secretsdump.py) and [LSA/cached-logon implementation](https://github.com/fortra/impacket/blob/master/impacket/examples/secretsdump.py) confirm LOCAL behavior, SECURITY parsing and conditional `.cached`/`.secrets` exports. Microsoft's [resultant password policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/activedirectory/get-aduserresultantpasswordpolicy), [resultant-PSO attribute](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/adschema/a-msds-resultantpso), [fine-grained policy guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/get-started/adac/fine-grained-password-policies) and [lockout-threshold semantics](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/security-policy-settings/account-lockout-threshold) support the policy interpretation. **Corrections and interpretation.** Page 2's prose calls the web service Apache, while its scan reports Werkzeug. Its `10.10.11.435` RPC address is malformed. Page 14 calls `/home/keira/user.txt` a root flag; it is the user path shown in the session.

A log showing an unqualified Git helper is not sufficient by itself to prove exploitable elevated PATH resolution, and a newly downloaded local binary does not establish the restricted target binary's version or behavior. For packages, makepkg consumes PKGBUILD and builds the archive; pacman installs it. Package `post_install` scriptlets and ALPM post-transaction hooks are separate mechanisms. The dummy tar archive is not referenced by the displayed empty `source=()` recipe and is not established as necessary. `--skipinteg` bypasses checks and was not imported. The final screenshot shows both set-user-ID and set-group-ID effects; these were treated as historical evidence rather than packaged as a system-modification procedure.

**Corrections and interpretation.** Pages 2â€“3 vary an HTTP Host header; the result is virtual-host comparison, not evidence that public DNS contains those names. A 400 response from one candidate is still a response distinction worth examining. Existing Wfuzz guidance already teaches baseline controls, word-count filters and individual confirmation. The document's motivation says the disclosures lack CVEs, while its synopsis names them; these are historical source statements, not a current vulnerability inventory or patch assessment.

Pages 9â€“17 distinguish task metadata, artifact bytes and deserialization. The historical ClearML SDK's `get()` selects behavior using the artifact type and can fall back to a local Path. The first Path result from a `custom` artifact does not itself demonstrate double serialization; the later explicit pickle-type/Path serialization example is different. A dictionary check after deserialization cannot prevent side effects that occurred while loading. The upload transformation shown in the source is SDK logic, so attributing it solely to the remote backend is misleading. The shown artifact-metadata update is an authenticated API request for the created task; by itself it does not demonstrate an unauthenticated or cross-user fileserver write. Pages 18â€“21 show a wrapper that rejects only `OVERTLY_MALICIOUS`, yet the accepted candidate is explicitly `LIKELY_UNSAFE`. This is an acceptance-policy gap, not evidence that the scanner declared it safe. Scanner exit status, report validity and all relevant records must survive the wrapper. Modern Fickling CLI source rejects findings above `LIKELY_SAFE`, and JSON output appends a result for each stacked pickle; a stale file or single-object parser could distort coverage. The ordinary CLI decompiles symbolically, whereas the similarly named library loading functions can actually deserialize. Model accuracy and an apparently successful evaluation do not prove that loading lacked side effects.

The writeup overgeneralises old `.pt` files as tar and newer `.pth` files as ZIP. Inspect actual formats: PyTorch has multiple historical representations, and extensions do not select them. Current PyTorch documentation also changes the context of the historical `torch.load` call: since 2.6 the default is weights-only when no pickle module is supplied, with documented remaining risks. No assertion is made that current tools reproduce the historical bypass. The failed web redirects for the rendered serialization page were resolved by reading the project's documentation source.

Pages 3â€“9 distinguish an injected HTML result, a blocked inline script and the later same-origin uploaded-script alert. Pages 10â€“17 describe application-specific authenticated script requests, basket identifiers and download handling. The initial textual decoding of a PDF/ZIP response is not a faithful binary capture; the later blob approach avoids that text conversion. The shared FormData object in the loop accumulates fields and should not be treated as a clean reusable uploader. Pages 18â€“22 correlate a loopback listener, forwarding, process identity and application source. The find command selects directories with an other-read mode bit, not all files readable by everyone. The displayed Node.js `spawn` uses an argument array without enabling a shell; inadequate path validation does not by itself establish shell-command injection. Output extension handling explains why an extensionless destination can become an OEB directory. On pages 23â€“26, a password prompt after offering a key does not uniquely diagnose a missing authorized_keys file. Page 24's screenshot says `Cannot POST /convert`; that HTTP 404 does not prove a particular output-file rejection. The later file listing and successful response are separate evidence. No symlink, permission or authorized-key change was reproduced.

Pages 27â€“33 show a privileged Python wrapper interpolating an SQL argument, inserting returned text into a PostScript template and invoking ps2pdf with NOSAFER. An unchanged generated template on page 29 does not establish that the intended row was returned. Page 30's rendered result identifies MariaDB 10.3.38; this is more specific evidence than the application connector's name. Page 32 shows the changed rendering, followed by a separate file-write/SSH sequence in the source. The wrapper's test of stdout alone is not a conversion-status check: the child return status, diagnostics and final artifact have distinct meanings. No SQL injection, PostScript file-write payload or privileged generator execution was adopted into the skills.

Pages 8â€“10 establish the outer form encoding and inner base64/XML representation. The `%2B`/`%3D` layer must be handled before decoding base64, while a second form decode can corrupt a recovered plus sign. GNU `--wrap=0` disables output wrapping; it does not URL-encode the result. The new curl adaptation lets `--data-urlencode name@file` perform that outer layer exactly once. The supplied XXE payload and response show a case-specific file disclosure; an XML parser's resource support, process permissions and character/content restrictions limit any general "read any file" claim.

The displayed script is root-owned and readable, with an eval call shown separately; the PDF does not include the entire validator source, so unshown parsing steps were not invented. `int(ticketCode) % 7 == 4` means remainder four, not divisibility by seven. The catalogue now contains **122 independent skills**. The new command forms are documentation-derived adaptations, not claims that the PDF used them or that they were executed locally. No review footer or shared runtime dependency was added.

**Corrections and interpretation.** Page 1 outlines the guest-SMB, captured-authentication, service-key, SQL and Windows escalation chain. Page 2 uses Nmap default TCP discovery before a version/script follow-up; that is not all-ports coverage. Human-output filtering and a SQL Server RTM banner do not establish complete service or patch coverage. Page 3's `tee /etc/hosts` command lacks append mode and would replace the file; it was not adopted or executed. The actual NetExec flag shown is `--shares`, despite singular prose. The later smbclient prompt names the client's default identity, so the earlier guest result does not establish that the two sessions used the same principal.

Pages 4â€“5 show an uploaded Internet Shortcut whose icon points to a literal UNC address, followed by SMB NTLMv2-SSP output. That route need not rely on name poisoning. Upload success alone does not establish that a particular person opened the file or requested authentication. The captured value is a challenge-response record, not a raw NT password hash; the PDF truncates the displayed record and therefore does not supply a usable complete fixture. Responder's unrestricted defaults were replaced with explicit mode/module decisions. Analyze mode only suppresses selected name-poisoning behavior; independently enabled SMB and other servers can still collect authentication. A running main process does not prove each requested listener bound successfully.

Pages 5â€“6 show the reported recovered credential, broad BloodHound collection and a GetUserSPNs request for `MSSQLSvc/breachdc.breach.vl:1433`. Existing BloodHound/GetUserSPNs guidance already covers bounded collection and TGS evidence. The displayed absence of a credential cache does not negate a subsequently returned TGS record. The graph's KRBTGT node and narrative about automatic rotation do not establish a password-change schedule; no unsupported rotation claim was transferred.

Page 7 uses a known service password with `pypykatz crypto nt`: this computes MD4 over the exact UTF-16LE password bytes, without a trailing null. The resulting NT key also serves RC4-HMAC, but it is not an AES key or a NetNTLMv2 response. The source ticket command omits the port displayed in the preceding SPN and changes the DC address; neither discrepancy was copied as a portable convention. The domain SID is distinct from an account RID. Current ticketer defaults include RID 500, multiple privileged groups and a ten-year lifetime; the authored fixture explicitly sets those fields. Current cache-saving code can import an inherited cache, so the scoped subshell clears that variable before creating a fresh fixture. Keytab use and current options were checked against upstream code; the source screenshot is an older Impacket version.

Pages 8â€“9 show a saved cache and SQL connection. A TLS-upgrade message is not successful SQL authentication, and a saved ticket does not prove its signature or target acceptance. The SQL prompt identifies a login/database context; it does not identify the OS token used by a command launched by the service. The source changes advanced options and xp_cmdshell with RECONFIGURE, then prints the service-account identity. The accompanying NULL row does not invalidate the preceding identity row. Current helpers also change advanced options, so disabling a helper is not proof that original configuration was restored.

Page 10 shows SeImpersonatePrivilege and a Windows-only GodPotato payload followed by a SYSTEM callback. A listed privilege alone is not proof that a particular exploit is compatible with every Windows version or service context. PowerShell's `curl` spelling is not evidence of GNU curl semantics. These observations were read for context; no payload, reverse connection, privileged service change or target authentication was executed.

**Reviewed without additional changes / deliberately deferred.** Existing Nmap, NetExec, smbclient, BloodHound, GetUserSPNs, Hashcat's Kerberoast workflow, netcat and basic HTTP-server guidance already cover the reusable portions of their appearances. The GUI graph workflow, client-side shortcut trigger, xp_cmdshell enablement/payload sequence, PowerShell callback and Windows-only GodPotato chain were not expanded into new Linux tool recipes. A separate Windows execution skill would require appropriate platform scope and fixtures. All PDF pages were covered; the truncated challenge-response and payload text were not reconstructed or claimed as runnable evidence.

**Page coverage and corrections.** Pages 1â€“2 identify the source and historical Windows web-application chain. Pages 3â€“8 cover Nmap, library pages, path discovery, registration, role listings and another directory scan. The Nmap command explicitly requests all TCP ports, but a service guess marked `mysql?` is not confirmation of an authenticated database. Gobuster's fifty-thread setting is source context, not a universally appropriate request rate. A zero-byte PHP response does not establish an empty source file, and a listed admin name is not authorization to act as that identity.

Pages 9â€“11 show a quoted-title result, intercepted book requests, traversal-based file disclosure and PHP source. A search returning a title with an apostrophe does not prove the implementation escaped input or that every SQL-injection path is absent. The disclosed win.ini and PHP bytes support this endpoint's file-read observation; they do not establish arbitrary code execution merely because a PHP file was read. Returned escaped source text must be decoded accurately before review.

Pages 12â€“14 show a session-ID generator selecting one username character and hashing fixed surrounding text, followed by candidate requests and an observed changed session. Its possible suffixes are bounded by distinct username characters, rather than a large random secret space. The script labels every non-302 response a valid session; that heuristic also admits errors or denials and was not adopted. PHP's Location header does not itself terminate execution. A candidate identifier only retrieves authenticated state if the application has corresponding saved session data; constructing the identifier does not populate that state.

Pages 15â€“16 show why access to the file-management page did not establish upload permission: the handler separately checks a nested JWT username and the server session. The hardcoded hex-looking secret is used as literal text by the displayed application. Existing jwt-tool guidance already covers exact key-file bytes and signature-versus-acceptance limits; this intake adds the independent session gate. Browser cookie edits, secret values and forged source-case tokens were not copied into runtime examples.

Pages 17â€“18 show multipart upload handling, an executed PHP payload and a PowerShell callback. A client-supplied MIME label or filename is not server validation. The prose's claim that renaming a function evades AMSI was not generalized into guidance: the provided session output establishes only the historical observed session, not a reliable detection guarantee. No bypass, payload download, upload or callback was performed. Pages 19â€“20 show a credential-containing JSON-like excerpt and a later SSH identity result; the excerpt includes trailing commas and is not a strict JSON fixture. Stored password-looking text and actual authentication evidence remain separate observations. Page 20's screenshot was read explicitly despite having no extracted text.

Pages 21â€“22 show a task note about password storage, a Sticky Notes directory and SQLite results. The directory contains a 4 KiB main database, a much larger WAL and a shared-memory sidecar. The existing SQLite/scp skills already require a consistent acquisition and warn that copying changing files independently is not a backup. Successful inspection here does not prove the wildcard transfer was atomic or that a modern app uses the same schema/path. The broad `SELECT *` was not repeated where bounded, schema-led queries are already documented.

Pages 23â€“24 show the downloaded binary, its ELF classification, decompiler output and Windows netstat listing. The screenshot is unambiguously ELF 64-bit x86-64, contradicting the 32-bit sentence. A Linux binary stored on Windows is not a Windows executable. The hardcoded hostname described as a cloud service ultimately leads to an observed loopback listener; the phrase alone is not evidence of public hosting. The libcurl form body is a clue to application inputs, not proof of the full server query. Existing SSH guidance already preserves listener scope, remote-loopback meaning and application hostname when forwarding.

Pages 25â€“27 show a form response, UNION-based data retrieval, a pyaes block-decryption loop, padded output and a subsequent administrator login. The first table-enumeration command as printed lacks its closing shell quote; it was not copied. AES alone does not establish CBC, an IV or a KDF. The reviewed pyaes constructor uses a zero IV when omitted and its low-level decrypt method returns whole blocks without removing padding. The source's displayed repeated trailing byte is consistent with PKCS#7; the new procedure checks the actual padding rule rather than simply ignoring arbitrary suffix bytes. No source-case ciphertext or credential was decrypted or authenticated locally.

Ghidra appears as a GUI analysis step without a supported headless task, so no CLI skill was invented from it. PyJWT and pyaes are used as Python libraries; neither justified a separate command-line package here. Session enumeration, traversal reads, web-shell upload, AMSI evasion, UNION extraction and Windows-specific remote execution were read as source context and deliberately not executed or expanded into additional recipes. **Coverage and corrections.** Pages 1â€“2 identify the case and show all-TCP discovery followed by service/script scanning. The screenshot reports Nginx 1.18.0 with HTTP 401 and ActiveMQ OpenWire 5.15.15 on TCP 61616. These are separate services; the HTTP response does not establish OpenWire authentication. The search phrase on page 2 incorrectly says CVE-2023-46606; the surrounding explanation, linked repository and Apache advisory identify **CVE-2023-46604**. Apache describes the Java OpenWire marshaller and affected clients as well as brokers, with branch fixes including 5.15.16. The version banner remains evidence to corroborate against the deployed build, not a reason to execute a proof of concept.

Pages 3â€“4 show generation of an ELF callback, a Spring XML payload, a Python HTTP server, Netcat and execution of a Go proof of concept. The embedded download uses `curl -s` without HTTP failure handling, and semicolons do not gate later commands on download success. The sender's packet message alone does not prove target execution. The separate listener screenshot includes a PTY command and `uid=1000(activemq)`, which support the historical case's reported session. These screenshots were read directly because extraction omitted the results. Existing Go, Python server, Ncat and script guidance already covers the reusable mechanics; no payload was executed or retained as a new recipe.

Page 5's screenshot shows `(ALL : ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/sbin/nginx` without an argument restriction. The important authority is selecting configuration and its included/native resources, not merely skipping a password prompt. The source then combines root workers, a filesystem-wide HTTP root and DAV PUT; these are distinct directives and prerequisites. Nginx `user` controls workers, while `root` maps request paths. Neither a parent master running as root nor a root-looking path alone establishes the request's actual permissions. The general skill teaches those distinctions without providing the privileged replacement configuration.

Pages 5â€“6 start an additional instance through `-c`; that is not a test or reload of an existing master. The `ss` output shows an IPv4 wildcard listener on 1337 with no process details. It does not prove ownership, which configuration is loaded, remote reachability or successful writes. The source leaves parent-directory creation unspecified; standard DAV defaults require existing parents unless `create_full_put_path` is enabled. Included-module availability, request-body temporary storage and destination permissions remain consequential conditions. Existing ss guidance already covers socket visibility and namespace limits.

Pages 6â€“7 create an SSH key pair, issue a PUT and show a later root SSH identity. The source uses shell command substitution to construct the body, which removes trailing newlines, and does not capture an HTTP status. Curl's quiet completion alone would be insufficient write evidence; the later displayed `uid=0` is separate historical evidence. PUT can replace the destination rather than append a line. The accepted upload example uses a user-selected ordinary file/URL and explains byte preservation and uncertain outcomes, without reproducing an authorized_keys write or attempting a login.

**Reviewed without changes / deliberately deferred.** Existing Nmap, Go, Python HTTP server, Ncat, script, ss, SSH and ssh-keygen cover recurring selection, scope, session and transfer decisions. ActiveMQ appears as a remote service and proof-of-concept target, not an administrative CLI workflow; no generic ActiveMQ skill was invented. The source's exploit download/build, msfvenom callback, Spring process launch, privileged Nginx startup, credential-file replacement and root login were studied as context and deliberately not executed or packaged as new payload instructions. No pages were left unread.

Pages 15â€“16 show pspy v1.2.0 observing UID 0 commands, including a timeout-wrapped Bash renewal job. UID metadata does not itself prove script-file ownership, writability or exact argv boundaries. The source's Ctrl-Z-and-restart advice can leave a collector suspended; the accepted correction directs inspection of the original instance first. The displayed `bash -c` command line lacks preserved argument boundaries, so the caller's source is needed before inferring which value reached the script as `$1`.

Pages 16â€“18 show the renewal excerpt, a one-day generated certificate, a command-bearing subject and later root identity. The script treats any nonzero checkend result as a path toward renewal, even though malformed input also produces nonzero. Its own `exit 1` for 'no need to renew' is the wrapper's convention, not OpenSSL's success convention. The injection arises when certificate text is reparsed by a child Bash; OpenSSL does not execute the CN. The source's `-keyout /dev/null` discards the private key and does not produce a reusable certificate/key pair; current OpenSSL documents `-nodes` as a deprecated synonym for `-noenc`. The later file ownership and root callback are historical observations only, not tests run here.

Pages 5â€“6 build the purported PNG prefix as a Python 3 Unicode string containing seven characters followed by a newline. That final newline makes eight characters, but UTF-8 encoding expands U+0089 to two bytes. Current Requests passes string-valued file content into urllib3's multipart encoder, whose string writer uses UTF-8; under that path the prefix becomes nine bytes starting `c2 89`. The W3C signature is eight bytes starting `89 50`, and even its exact presence does not make a complete PNG. The historical library versions and transmitted body were not supplied, so this is a source-supported current behavior and a reproduction caveat, not a recovered packet capture. The source's unconditional `Uploaded!` print does not check the HTTP or application result. Later screenshots report command execution, which is separate evidence from the claimed image-validation explanation.

Pages 6â€“7 show curl requests, a temporary HTTP server, a downloaded Windows Netcat executable and the reported session as `buff\shaun`. They were read without sending requests, transferring executables or starting listeners. No web-shell body or case credential was added to the skills.

Page 8 shows `CloudMe_1112.exe` in Downloads and a Windows netstat line with local address `127.0.0.1:8888`; the `0.0.0.0:0` foreign-address column is not the bind address. The installer filename is a version lead, while that netstat output alone does not identify the owning process or running build. The PDF describes a local installation in a VM but supplies no debugger derivation of the later offset/address.

Page 9 calls the connection a SOCKS proxy, but its remote syntax specifies a fixed reverse TCP forward to client loopback port 8888. It also says port 8080 in prose while the command uses 8888; the Chisel transport uses 9999. The displayed connection message establishes transport progress, not an application response. The accepted skill already used explicit loopback binding, authentication and a trusted fingerprint; those conditions were preserved.

Pages 9â€“10 display a generated reverse payload with callback port 4444, then a listener on 2222 and a reported administrator session. The callback host also differs from the earlier Chisel server host. Different hosts can be intentional, but the PDF does not reconcile this sequence, and the differing ports cannot be silently treated as one verified transcript. A fixed forward does not automatically rewrite a separate outbound connection's endpoint.

Page 11 supplies the complete appendix code: fixed padding, a hard-coded return address, payload bytes, a remaining-length calculation and a socket send. It was read as source evidence without execution. These build-specific constants and the source's Python 2 invocation do not demonstrate a portable exploit or a validated debugging workflow.

**Reviewed without changes / deliberately deferred.** Existing `xxd`, `searchsploit` and `msf-pattern` coverage already supplies exact-byte interpretation, applicability review and independently established offsets. No new debugger, payload generator or Windows netstat skill was inferred from mere mentions. Full application upload behavior, the exact CloudMe build, offset/address derivation and the inconsistent callback transcript would require controlled fixtures and original versions. They remain explicitly unverified; page coverage is complete. No exploitation, payload construction, authentication or remote operation ran.

**Primary verification.** PHP's [POST upload fields](https://www.php.net/manual/en/features.file-upload.post-method.php) and [move_uploaded_file](https://www.php.net/manual/en/function.move-uploaded-file.php) establish client control of the MIME field, HTTP upload provenance, result semantics and destination behavior. Chisel's [upstream usage](https://github.com/jpillora/chisel#usage) establishes remote syntax, reverse direction, default bind behavior and the explicit SOCKS variant. Python's [binary I/O](https://docs.python.org/3.12/library/functions.html#open) and [bytes/encoding documentation](https://docs.python.org/3.12/library/stdtypes.html#bytes-objects), plus the [PNG signature specification](https://www.w3.org/TR/png-3/#5PNG-file-signature), support the byte-inspection procedure. The current [Requests multipart preparation source](https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/_modules/requests/models/) and [urllib3 multipart encoder](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/urllib3/urllib3/main/src/urllib3/filepost.py) support the encoding caveat. **Coverage and corrections.** Pages 1â€“4 introduce the case, show SSH/HTTP enumeration, reveal client-side JavaScript credentials and try login/discovery requests. Literal browser-side comparisons are visible source evidence; one rejected payload does not prove that every server-side path is safe. The printed hosts-file command has problematic formatting and elevates printf rather than the shell redirection; it was not reused or executed. A MySQL version banner is evidence about the database response, not proof of an exact OpenEMR patch level. The prose's user_secure spelling differs from the displayed users_secure table. Page 12 displays several HashID labels and a subsequent John bcrypt recovery. Pattern matches do not prove the originating application, and multiple labels can describe the same format family. Current upstream HashID omits the bcrypt 2b prefix from its recognition expression; the skill records that concrete compatibility issue without prescribing mutation of the acquired value. The case's password recovery was read but not reproduced. Existing John bcrypt guidance already covers full records, cost and bounded recovery.

Pages 13â€“16 describe five application-side execution routes, including file editing, uploads, document templates and legacy exploit scripts. Directory listing by itself does not prove server-side execution; the source provides separate execution output for one route. Those mechanisms were read as evidence, but no PHP payload, Python 2 exploit invocation, remote upload or reverse connection was executed or added as a reusable procedure.

Page 17 shows an interactive shell and a local account switch. Its success does not retroactively explain the earlier SSH failure because authentication paths and policy can differ. Pages 18â€“19 then show Memcached statistics, key listing and a selected value. The displayed STAT items:1:number 5 means five stored items in slab class 1, contrary to the prose's claim of a single item numbered 1. The zero in stats cachedump 1 0 removes the requested item-count limit; server implementation limits still apply. Current upstream walks the cold LRU and caps the response buffer, so this legacy listing is not a complete inventory. The VALUE header's zero is opaque flags and its nine is a byte count excluding framing. One quit closes the connection; sending it twice is not a protocol requirement. Cached authentication-looking data does not itself prove that any login is currently valid.

Pages 19â€“21 show docker group membership, an Ubuntu image, a host-root bind mount, chroot and a reported root password change/login. The explanation incorrectly relies on the Docker client being SUID. A rootful daemon's authority and access to its API/socket explain the relevant privilege boundary. Group membership alone still needs effective identity, context and actual daemon-access evidence, and rootless mode changes the authority model. No host-root mount, chroot, password change or authentication was attempted.

Pages 18â€“19 contain a more useful source-review lesson. Its grep command treats captured PHP output as a filename, so an error can select the restore branch even if the marker was present. The checksum covers the launcher, while the launcher's include resolves another file. That is a dependency-integrity gap, not a demonstrated MD5 collision. The appended PHP statement is also printed without a terminating semicolon; its complete surrounding source would be required to establish executable syntax. The helper decodes base64, converts literal key/IV strings to UTF-8 bytes and selects CBC. The displayed code omits a padding assignment; standard .NET symmetric-algorithm defaults use PKCS7. It allocates plaintext storage to ciphertext length, ignores the returned read count and decodes the whole buffer, which can append NULs. **Page coverage and corrections.** Pages 1â€“3 give the attack narrative, a top-1000 TCP scan, exposed Git metadata, the downloader and web enumeration. The scan's two open ports describe that tested set, not all possible listeners. A denied `.git/` index does not make individual objects inaccessible. Current upstream git-dumper invokes Git checkout automatically, modifies potentially unsafe config lines and warns that attacker-controlled content can execute locally. Its normal HTTP sessions disable certificate verification, and its non-directory-listing path ignores checkout status. The accepted skill therefore separates endpoint identity, isolation, transfer status and recovered-object completeness; no downloader invocation was performed. Pages 4â€“6 show registration, a GET request with credentials in its query string and an upload result. HTTP method alone does not establish the backend's account-lookup/create logic. A query string can be recorded by the configured log format; it is not proof that every service logs passwords. Pages 7â€“9 compare a blacklist and different HTML output paths, then build an event-handler payload. The prose sometimes calls this a filename injection, but the illustrated altered `alt` attribute and multipart `cat_name` field show the display-name flow; the image filename is separate. The accepted PHP guidance preserves that distinction and explains why encoding on the admin list does not establish encoding on the detail page. Existing binary/upload guidance already separates GIF/PNG labels and prefixes from valid image content.

Pages 10â€“12 show the recovered browser session, a concatenated INSERT, separately bound DELETE, SQLite ATTACH statements and a web-shell/reverse-connection sequence. The later bound statement does not protect the earlier concatenation. ATTACH is a database/file operation, not intrinsic OS command execution: the historical outcome also depends on the application's SQL API, filesystem permissions, served path and PHP execution mapping. The initial generic file path and adapted application path differ. Binary-looking response prefixes should be captured to a file rather than forced to a terminal. No SQL injection, database write, web shell, server, reverse connection or payload execution was attempted.

Pages 13â€“15 export users, transform delimiters, run John, inspect groups and read Apache logs. Raw-MD5 was not selected from length alone in the new guidance; identical-length NT or other records require origin evidence. The displayed export has ten rows while the loader reports nine records; the source does not supply enough run state to resolve that difference. The skill already separates loader input, duplicate/pot state and `--show` results, now with an explicit record-association reminder. A home-directory name or database account is not automatically an OS login identity. The log directory and files show group ownership plus usable permission bits; the name `adm` alone is not a universal read grant. A logged submitted value and a redirect response are not proof of authentication; later successful source-case `su` is separate evidence. No hashes or logged credentials were used here.

Pages 18â€“19 send a review link, fetch a private-repository file through a browser session, decode a not-found response, then fetch a different file and reuse a discovered value. The mail clue names `README.md`, while the failed request uses `readme.md`; case-sensitive repository paths are a plausible additional explanation, so the failure does not establish absence of the named README. The script does not preserve the original fetch status. A callback's 200 is the collector's response status, and successful base64 decoding can merely recover an error body. Existing curl/base64 guidance covers that evidence distinction. Browser-session actions, private-file exfiltration and root credential reuse were deliberately not turned into utility defaults or executed. PHP's [htmlspecialchars manual](https://www.php.net/manual/en/function.htmlspecialchars.php), [CLI options](https://www.php.net/manual/en/features.commandline.options.php) and [PDO prepare documentation](https://www.php.net/manual/en/pdo.prepare.php) support the explicit encoding check, PHP 8.1 default change and actual parameter-binding boundary. [SQLite ATTACH documentation](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_attach.html), [Apache log-format documentation](https://httpd.apache.org/docs/2.4/mod/mod_log_config.html) and [Gitea's 1.22.1 announcement](https://blog.gitea.com/release-of-1.22.1/) bound source-case claims without asserting target execution.

README catalogue entries were updated. Both new packages contain only their own SKILL.md and have no shared runtime dependency. Existing SSH forwarding, John key-format handling and scan guidance already cover their corresponding tasks; no redundant examples or separate Web3 SDK package were added.

**Page coverage and source qualifications.** Pages 1â€“2 introduce the two Ethereum-backed applications, IPFS and filesystem slack. Page 3 shows an all-TCP scan followed by selected-port service/default-script probing. Anonymous FTP returns Solidity source, a JSON artifact and an address file; an unclassified port is not itself proof of Ethereum. The existing scan guidance already handles scope and uncertain service classification.

Pages 4â€“5 show a string getter and setter and their ABI descriptions. An ABI specifies encoding/decoding; a matching filename does not prove that it describes deployed bytecode at a particular address. Pages 6â€“7 construct a Web3.py client, select the first exposed account and read a getter. Client construction does not load or verify every storage value, and an account in an RPC list is not proof of an unlocked signer. The old camelCase API is generation-specific; it was not copied into a new Python skill. The Cast adaptation checks the chosen chain/address/block and separates decode or missing-state errors from valid values.

Page 8 submits a transaction, reads the updated string and shows two ICMP request/reply pairs in tcpdump. The changed value and observed traffic are separate evidence stages; a submitted transaction hash is not by itself a mined successful receipt, and a getter does not prove an operating-system consumer executed the returned text. The historical local chain may mine immediately; portable guidance must not assume that timing. Page 9 shows a reverse-shell identity and a passwd excerpt. Contrary to the prose claiming only bobby has a Bash shell, the screenshot also assigns `/bin/bash` to administrator. Account shell metadata is separate from current SSH access policy. No payload or network probe was executed.

Page 10 enumerates the local IPFS store, loops over CIDs with `ipfs ls` and suppresses errors. IPFS does not require a blockchain, contrary to the source's description. The historical `Qm...` inventory representation differs from current Kubo's raw-codec CIDv1 inventory; not every stored block is a complete named file or UnixFS directory. The new guidance retains errors and obtains correctly typed root CIDs from known references/pins/MFS rather than blindly replaying the loop. A missing HTTP gateway does not by itself establish that all CLI operations stay offline.

Page 11 shows a multipart email's header excerpt, followed by a claimed extracted attachment decode and SSH-key recovery. The displayed header excerpt is insufficient to reproduce the exact attachment extraction: the part body and relevant part headers are omitted. `X-Attached` and `.enc` do not establish Content-Transfer-Encoding or encryption. Base64 decoding is separate from parsing/decrypting the resulting key; MIME tools may already have decoded it. The John output warns of possible candidate false positives. Page 12 then shows a distinct successful SSH identity observation; no recovered secret or authentication was reused here.

Page 13 shows a root-owned SUID executable and contract source containing application state. A failed password search does not establish that a hash cannot be cracked. Pages 14â€“15 show an application credential rejection, a generated address file, a loopback listener, SSH local forwarding and SCP. The unprivileged netstat output explicitly lacks some process attribution. A listening socket and a functioning forward do not independently establish the application protocol; the existing SSH package already explains both ends and destination failures.

Page 16 hardcodes a different contract address from the address displayed on page 14, despite prose saying it came from that file. Portable instructions use the actual deployment evidence. Pages 16â€“17 change application credentials and then receive an approval failure. Page 18 changes approval and receives an insufficient-funds message; these responses describe different application checks, not a universal login model. Pages 18â€“19 show a transfer predicate requiring a positive amount no greater than the remaining totalSupply. The page 19 explanation reverses the comparison in prose. Its contract balance is application state, not automatically the account's native-currency balance, and rerunning the same transfer after supply changes can behave differently. The later root `id` is an independent observed outcome of the source's SUID program. No contract transaction, financial transfer or SUID execution was performed.

Pages 19â€“20 compare a logical file read with `bmap --mode slack`. The shown file size is 52 bytes, filesystem block size 4096 and trailing slack 4044. This concerns bytes after EOF in an allocated filesystem block, not slack in RAM. Copying the logical file normally does not retain that original allocation/tail. The skill's arithmetic example is labelled illustrative and does not claim a recovered artifact. The source's final fragment is a finding within that lab, not a generally valid interpretation of any readable slack bytes.

**Primary verification, reviewed 2026-10-10.** The [Kubo CLI reference](https://docs.ipfs.tech/reference/kubo/cli/) verifies offline mode, timeouts, local inventory, recursive-pin listing, MFS listing/stat, UnixFS ls and cat byte limits. The [refs source](https://github.com/ipfs/kubo/blob/master/core/commands/refs.go) and CLI notes qualify raw block inventory and possible online retrieval. [Basic CLI operations](https://docs.ipfs.tech/how-to/kubo-basic-cli/) distinguishes directories and files; [IPFS concepts](https://docs.ipfs.tech/concepts/what-is-ipfs/) supplies the content-addressed model. Its [bmap.c](https://github.com/CameronLonsdale/bmap/blob/master/bmap.c) verifies the read-only raw-device open for slack mode, regular-file check, terminal-block calculation, source-mutating alternate modes, append behavior of `--outfile` and unchecked raw I/O/exit-status limitations. Pages 8â€“10 describe a 16-character zero-filled decimal byte count followed by a 16-byte IV and CBC ciphertext. The code uses a 65,536-byte read buffer, despite page 9 incorrectly describing 64*1024 bits as 16 bytes. Padding applies when the chunk length is not a multiple of 16, not merely when a chunk is shorter than 16. The source's SHA-256 digest is a 32-byte AES key. The original length is significant for removing space padding; calling it insignificant on page 10 loses that information. The decryption listing's text-mode open is not suitable for Python 3 binary ciphertext. A missing IV does not universally prevent recovery of every CBC block: later blocks depend on the preceding ciphertext. The added interpretation reflects that limit without treating unauthenticated output as trustworthy.

Page 11 prints readable inner base64 output followed by invalid input. Space padding plausibly explains the source symptom, but the supplied encrypted attachment is absent and was not reconstructed. The accepted workflow validates the established envelope, retains exactly the recorded original bytes, then checks the inner decoder's status. A visible plaintext prefix is not complete success. The local synthetic tests below independently verified the partial-output behavior; they do not reproduce the source artifact.

Pages 12â€“14 show a PDF web form, JavaScript/Ajax request, pdfTeX log, blacklist rejection, a different execution primitive and a shell. The log explicitly shows write18 enabled. This is evidence about the observed engine configuration and wrapper, not proof that every LaTeX package permits command execution. The page 14 log includes an executed identity before a later fatal PDF-generation error; failed final output does not undo an earlier side effect. No payload, compiler, network listener or shell callback was executed during ingestion.

Pages 15â€“16 show restricted Bash rejecting cd and a slash-containing command-not-found handler. A later diagnostic explicitly says ls is absent from PATH; this is more precise than saying ls itself is restricted. The tar checkpoint creates a child shell in the source and does not itself change the user identity. PATH remains limited, and a subsequently started shell presents another PATH value; interpreter startup must be checked independently. The new Bash addition teaches diagnosis, not the escape payload. Existing tar extraction scope was left intact.

Page 17's ZIP capture reports unreadable/skipped files, and displayed source/destination sizes differ. The transfer is therefore not demonstrated to be a complete byte-identical profile acquisition. The source still shows an index and one profile directory. Page 18 uses a known profile password and outputs a saved Webmin login; that historical site record alone does not establish an OS root credential or current validity. The subsequent su session is separate evidence. Page 19 shows the Webmin command-shell interface and output, whose availability depends on the authenticated account's rights. No browser profile was opened or decrypted here and no recovered credential was tested.

The directly retrieved [CLI source](https://github.com/unode/firefox_decrypt/blob/main/firefox_decrypt.py) verifies explicit paths, list/choice handling, loading NSS before listing, direct profile fallback, stdin input, JSON fields, error branches and debug-secret exposure. The fetched source is 1,234 lines and differs from the older indexed web rendering; no downloaded source was imported or executed. [Mozilla profile documentation](https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/profiles-where-firefox-stores-user-data) identifies key4.db/logins.json. Source snapshot hashes are saved in ignored work.

The [OpenSSL s_client manual](https://docs.openssl.org/3.5/man1/openssl-s_client/) verifies SNI, hostname/trust enforcement, STARTTLS, CRLF and quiet/EOF handling. [RFC 9051](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9051.html) supplies mailbox state, tags, UIDVALIDITY, literal framing and read-only/PEEK behavior; [RFC 8314](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8314.html) confirms mail-TLS conventions. [WPScan enumeration source](https://github.com/wpscanteam/wpscan/blob/master/app/controllers/enumeration/cli_options.rb) confirms explicit user ranges and default sets; [WordPress content visibility](https://wordpress.org/documentation/article/content-visibility-classic-editor/) distinguishes protected content. **Page coverage and source qualifications.** Page 1 describes the Teampass, BookStack, SSH/TOTP and privileged checker stages. Page 2's scan header names heal.htb despite the Checker context; retain endpoint ambiguity instead of copying that name. The script's suggestion that an HTTP service might redirect does not prove an open proxy. Page 3's hosts-file example contains backticks inside double quotes, which would be shell substitution if pasted into Bash. No hosts-file mutation was made. Pages 6â€“7 alter a PHP filter-chain oracle request: nested base64 data is inserted in an image/body and a mapping is replaced by raw joined form fields. That construction does not generally preserve plus signs, ampersands or equals signs. The source's earlier POST description differs from its PUT implementation; page 8's captured save-draft request is PUT with JSON, whereas the later adaptation uses form encoding. A current method, body format, endpoint, session and CSRF value must be coherent. Creating a book/draft is a remote write, not passive request capture.

Page 9's command arguments and echoed headers show different CSRF/cookie values, so they are not a single literal reproducible session. The displayed passwd read is partial. Failure to retrieve the original authenticator path on page 10 does not prove that the file is universally absent or unprotected. The successful backup-path result establishes a different location in this case.

The page 10 screenshots explicitly contrast recursive copying with `--remove-destination -p` against `--remove-destination --no-preserve=mode,ownership`. The latter deliberately resets mode/ownership behavior; it is not equivalent to plain cp -r. Existing versus newly recreated destinations, umask, ACLs and parent-directory access matter. The new guidance uses a fresh private outer directory and archive preservation, then checks selected file metadata separately from bytes. Archive mode is not a consistent live-application snapshot and can suppress some extended-attribute/context preservation failures. Copying source/. can replace destination-directory metadata, so the private outer layer is retained when containment matters.

Pages 10â€“11 show a Base32 seed followed by a TOTP_AUTH configuration line, and then oathtool output with a leading zero. Only the seed is key input; the complete configuration file is not a Base32 key. Page 10's prose misspells the utility name, while page 11 shows oathtool. Code generation and the later successful SSH identity are separate evidence. The accepted skill requires known provisioning parameters and avoids secrets in arguments or verbose logs.

Page 11's sudo rule and Bash wrapper lead into page 12's checker outcomes. Sourcing .env executes shell code; a C getenv call additionally requires the relevant variables to be exported. The wrapper's filtered username does not establish trust in later data. A match against a particular leaked-hash list does not establish comprehensive password safety when no match is found. The HTTP server exposes its served directory, including configuration and hash files in the listing. No transfer-integrity hash is shown. These conditions are recorded without reproducing the service or transferring files.

Page 13's decompiled main obtains environment variables and enforces a maximum strlen of 0x14 bytes, not a universal twenty-character Unicode rule. Its database lookup fetches a password-hash field; a null result's meaning depends on omitted error handling. Page 14's main writes the shared-memory value, flushes output, sleeps, then calls notification and cleanup. This contradicts page 16's prose placing the write after the sleep. The source's 0x400 request is 1,024 bytes. The first shmget argument is a key; its return is the segment ID. Linux flag value 0x3b6 separates into IPC_CREAT and permissions 0666, not a sticky-bit file mode. IPC_EXCL is absent, so source alone does not prove that a fresh segment was created. ipcs provides a bounded way to inspect actual metadata; it was not run here.

Page 15 writes a timestamp/hash string, then reads and searches delimiters. The `+1` after the delimiter pointer already skips that delimiter before the trim helper; attributing the entire operation to trimming is inaccurate. Pages 16â€“17 contain an attack helper that changes shared memory and appends unchecked data. Its shmget flags do not reassign an existing segment's ownership or permissions. The helper was not compiled or executed. The subsequently constructed mysql invocation crosses OS-shell, client-command and SQL parsing layers; the system command runs under the client process on the client host, independently of server FILE privilege. Filtering the wrapper's username cannot sanitize the later shared-memory input.

Page 18 redirects output to a path called pipe, but does not demonstrate that the path is a FIFO. Buffering and scheduling prevent treating the displayed sequence as a reliable universal race recipe. The displayed SUID file mode and a later process's effective UID are separate observations. The May 31 file timestamp differs from the May 24 shared-memory display and May 28 cover date; the screenshots should not be treated as one verified timeline. No race, shell payload, permission change or privileged execution was performed.

**Primary verification, reviewed 2026-10-10.** The [OATH Toolkit manual](https://oath-toolkit.codeberg.page/oathtool.1.html) verifies stdin/file key input, Base32 versus hexadecimal, HOTP/TOTP modes, algorithms, time parameters and verbose-secret exposure. [RFC 6238 Appendix B](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6238.html#appendix-B) supplies the public SHA1 test vector (59 seconds, eight digits, expected 94287082); its clock/step requirements support the mismatch decision. This is a published reference value, not a locally captured result.

The upstream-authored [ipcs manual](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/ipcs.1.html) verifies resource/ID selection, mutually exclusive display formats and procfs fallback visibility. The [shmget manual](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/shmget.2.html), [Linux IPC flag header](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/include/uapi/linux/ipc.h), [shmat/shmdt manual](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/shmat.2.html) and [IPC namespace manual](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/ipc_namespaces.7.html) establish key/ID separation, creation versus permission bits, existing-segment behavior, attach/detach PID semantics and namespace scope. Metadata is not segment-content or last-writer evidence.

GNU's web manual could not be fetched directly. The [upstream coreutils manual source](https://github.com/coreutils/coreutils/blob/master/doc/coreutils.texi), saved under ignored work, and the upstream [cp option parser](https://github.com/coreutils/coreutils/blob/master/src/cp.c) / [copy implementation](https://github.com/coreutils/coreutils/blob/master/src/copy.c) verify preservation limits, destination removal and explicit non-preservation. The copy implementation applies default regular-file read/write permissions filtered by umask for newly created destinations under explicit no-preserve-mode. The manual distinguishes this from ordinary source-mode creation and existing destination behavior. No downloaded source was built or executed.

The [MySQL client-command manual](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/mysql-commands.html) and [client options](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/mysql-command-options.html) verify the local system command, formatting flags, noninteractive binary-mode exceptions and the 8.4.3/8.4.6 control additions. These version-specific controls are not assumed for MariaDB or historical clients; disabling client commands does not make arbitrary SQL harmless.

Existing nmap, sqlite3, hashcat, ss, ssh and ssh-keygen guidance already supports the scan coverage, structured record export, hash-mode/identity, socket ownership, forwarding and key-file decisions. **Page coverage and source qualifications.** Page 1 introduces two historical library vulnerabilities and a two-stage Nmap command. Its first scan does not request every TCP port; two displayed open services therefore do not establish complete TCP/UDP coverage. Parsing human-oriented scan output with grep/cut also needs a valid nonempty port list before the second scan. Existing nmap guidance covers these limits.

Page 2 identifies observed SSH/Werkzeug banners and shows registration/login followed by the CIF upload dashboard. Registration and upload mutate the application; a web-server banner does not identify the exact installed pymatgen dependency. Page 3's vulnerability screenshot and adapted CIF place an expression in a crystallographic transformation field. The root cause is unsafe evaluation inside a parser, not a rule that all text-based CIF files or all deserializers execute code. The accepted Python addition traces the actual library call and deployed version without parsing the suspect file.

Page 3's shell payload uses callback port 9000, while page 4's listener is on 9090. No intervening port mapping or correction is shown, so the transcript is not directly reproducible as printed. The payload is fetched and piped to a shell in the source; neither that command nor the parser, HTTP server, listener or callback was executed here. The page 4 uploaded-file screenshot shows a View action and the narrative associates that with parsing; merely accepting an upload does not independently establish execution.

Page 4 prints `script -c /dev/null bash`, reversing the intended roles for util-linux script: /dev/null becomes command text and bash becomes the transcript filename. The displayed prompt alone does not validate that invocation or complete terminal behavior. The existing skill already has the correct command and now makes argument roles explicit. The source's SQLite query requests every column from a user table and its continuation on page 5 contains fourteen records. The database file itself is not supplied. Existing sqlite3 guidance prefers read-only working copies, schema inspection and bounded structured output; splitting default output on a delimiter can corrupt fields or lose account association.

Page 5 shows four recovered candidates with Hashcat mode 0, an account-file grep and an SSH invocation followed by a rosa prompt for socket inspection. The hash display's length alone does not prove raw MD5, and matching a database hash is separate from current SSH acceptance. Filtering passwd for /bin/bash excludes other valid shell configurations. The ss display's Local Address column establishes a 127.0.0.1:8080 listener; the peer wildcard does not make it externally bound. Missing process details do not identify the owner. The forwarding command's destination loopback is resolved on the SSH server; current ssh/ss skills already cover binding, forwarding policy and application checks.

Page 6 claims authentication to the forwarded monitoring application and shows its dashboard, followed by an aiohttp 3.9.1 banner. The later Feroxbuster/curl commands do not show session credentials, so one cannot infer that each reused the browser's authenticated session or that all routes require authentication. The maintainer advisory requires a particular static-route configuration for CVE-2024-23334; a banner alone is insufficient. The scan reports automatic 404-like filtering and individual CSS resources, while /assets returns 403. Page 7 continues with accessible JavaScript children and denied parent paths. These results are compatible with disabled directory indexes; they do not establish the filesystem root or a vulnerability by themselves. Recheck a known child and a control under the same request context before changing filters or expanding discovery.

Page 7's displayed Bash conditional contains a Markdown-link-style suffix after the closing bracket. The defect is visible in the rendered PDF, not solely text extraction. It is not a directly executable Bash example as printed. Its loop discards one response body while reading status, then makes a second request for content. That pairs evidence from different transactions. The added curl guidance captures all response evidence in one fetch and explains the outgoing path change caused by --path-as-is. The source's three-ancestor success is case-specific and does not reveal a universal static-directory depth.

Pages 7â€“8 show a flag-like body and a truncated private-key block from paths outside the web root. Those displays support the source's claimed read primitive but do not independently identify the serving process as root or demonstrate shell execution. Page 8 ends with key permissions and an SSH command; it provides no resulting authenticated identity output. The incomplete key cannot be validated or used as a complete artifact, and no credential acquisition or login was attempted during ingestion.

**Primary verification, reviewed 2026-10-10.** The [curl option manual](https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html) verifies path normalization control, output/header capture, status reporting and transfer exit semantics. The [aiohttp static-file documentation](https://docs.aiohttp.org/en/stable/web_advanced.html#static-file-handling) confirms default directory-index denial, separate file serving and the significance of follow_symlinks. The [maintainer advisory](https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/security/advisories/GHSA-5h86-8mv2-jq9f) identifies the historical follow_symlinks=True condition, including cases without actual symlinks, and the 3.9.2 fix. No configuration change was applied.

The [pymatgen maintainer advisory](https://github.com/materialsproject/pymatgen/security/advisories/GHSA-vgv8-5cpj-qj2f) identifies JonesFaithfulTransformation.from_transformation_str and its unsafe eval despite __builtins__ being None. [Python's eval documentation](https://docs.python.org/3.12/library/functions.html#eval) confirms code execution and globals/builtins behavior. This supports source inspection rather than running a malicious CIF to establish a version finding. The upstream-authored [script manual](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/script.1.html) verifies command/transcript roles, child-status propagation and logging semantics. Relocated script history: documentation reviewed 2026-10-09, Linux execution untested, Altered p. 18, original source [util-linux script manual](https://github.com/util-linux/util-linux/blob/master/term-utils/script.1.adoc). No historical test result was upgraded.

The handler returned synthetic path/sequence markers and never read files. Default normalization sent /probe.txt; --path-as-is retained /docs/../probe.txt. Each capture made exactly one request and paired its headers/body/status. A complete HTTP 500 returned curl status 0; an intentionally short body retained HTTP 200 and partial bytes but returned curl status 18. The server was closed after testing. This verifies client request/capture behavior, not aiohttp routing, a vulnerable parser or the source target. Raw results are in ignored `runs/overnight-chemistry-2026-10-10/`.

Focused validators passed for curl, feroxbuster, python3 and script. The repository checker passed for **156 packages, 196 Markdown files, 244 local links and 356 Bash blocks**; Bash was parsed only. Catalogue membership and git diff --check passed, and the complete changed-content diff was reviewed. Feroxbuster and util-linux script were absent from PATH. No PTY/scanner/library runtime fixture, source database/hash recovery, target connection, Linux execution or worker evaluation occurred. The ignored per-file work directory retains extraction/page counts, all eight renders, relocated history, checks and review diff.

Deliberately deferred material: application registration/upload, malicious CIF construction/parsing, shell payload hosting or execution, listener/callback/TTY session, source database acquisition, password recovery/reuse, SSH forwarding or login, traversal against a real service, sensitive-file/key acquisition and privilege escalation. No tool installation, system/configuration change, original-PDF deletion/move, commit or push occurred. Unrelated edits and methodologies were preserved.

The catalogue now has 157 independent skills. Existing nmap and impacket-secretsdump guidance already covers scan completeness, source-store identity, paired hive prerequisites, NT-hash field selection and partial extraction. No duplicate whoami, native reg.exe or PowerShell package was created solely for this short Windows-side sequence. The Linux WinRM client skill contains the relevant remote token inspection.

**Page coverage and source qualifications.** Page 1 outlines the historical lab chain from AD/SMB discovery through credentials exposed in files/metadata, backup privileges and hash-based authentication. This is source narrative, not authorization to reproduce that chain. Page 2 shows Nmap 7.94SVN with -sC -sV -Pn, eleven open TCP ports and 989 filtered ports. The command does not request all TCP ports or UDP. DNS, LDAP, Kerberos and SMB observations support the AD hypothesis; they do not prove an exhaustive service inventory. The odd domain suffix in one LDAP banner should be reconciled with certificate/service names rather than copied blindly. TLS randomness explicitly does not represent time. Later WinRM access is not independently established by the displayed scan.

Page 3 appends a hosts entry and says there is no web interface, a conclusion wider than the shown scan proves. Its first CrackMapExec share request fails with STATUS_USER_SESSION_DELETED; an explicit guest/empty-password request then succeeds and lists HR and IPC$ as readable. These are distinct authentication contexts. Required SMB signing does not itself prevent permitted guest or named-account authentication. Share access labels are separate from permission to read a particular file.

Page 4's prose calls the smbclient connection guest, but its actual command omits -U and the password prompt identifies WORKGROUP\phoe. The transcript alone cannot establish which server-side identity was granted; mapping to guest or omitted context remains possible. The accepted addition makes the requested identity explicit. A quoted file name with spaces is downloaded, with a reported 1,266-byte size. The onboarding template contains an initial-password claim, not proof that every current user still accepts it. No source secret is copied into runtime examples.

Page 5 shows Impacket 0.12.0.dev1 lookupsid with explicit domain/guest and -no-pass, a reported domain SID and mixed user/group/alias rows. In particular, the DC computer account has a dollar suffix and SidTypeUser. This contradicts treating that type as a list of human users. The command's default RID bound cannot establish every directory account. Page 6 repeats the network operation to pipe names through grep/sed, losing domain/type context; the new skill instead keeps the original log and formats it offline. The prose also switches between user.txt and users.txt. The extracted list includes built-in, service and computer identities.

Page 6's password-spray output stops after the first displayed success, with later list entries unshown. That is evidence of the displayed successful pair, not evidence every account was tried or that all others failed. No spray was executed here. Page 7 uses --users and prints descriptions plus badpwdcount values, including a password-like description. Such metadata can be stale; a count is neither an account-policy decision nor a safe remaining-attempt budget. The new current-NetExec example requests one named user rather than assuming historical output or collecting the full domain.

Page 8 shows a different identity accessing DEV and retrieving a 601-byte PowerShell script. The source supplies its SMB password in the process arguments; the existing skill's prompt-based pattern avoids copying that approach. The page's final prose adds a trailing exclamation mark to the script credential that is absent from both the actual script and subsequent login command on page 9. That discrepancy is visible in the rendered source and was not normalized into a supposedly verified credential.

Page 9 constructs a PSCredential but never uses that variable in the shown backup action. Creating a credential object alone does not change the executing identity. An unconditional success-message statement after Compress-Archive is not independent evidence that an archive was created successfully. The strings output contains fragmented path/command text interleaved with extra characters; it guides disassembly but does not alone establish a complete executable command or code path.

Page 11 traces action 4, which the preceding README says deletes users. The observed setreuid call fails with EPERM, then access(path, R_OK) fails with EACCES; the program prints a combined unreadable/not-found message and exits zero. The trace proves an attempted permission check in that context, not a successful read or absence of the file. Ptrace can suppress set-ID transitions, and access normally checks real rather than effective IDs. A working privileged run cannot be inferred from this failed traced run. Retrying the same action without tracing could have destructive effects. The later path-traversal command shows a snipped private-key block, not a complete local key artifact. The proxy's displayed destination address differs from the earlier scan address, so those observations must keep their individual session context.
